Mr. Speaker, the government has
authorized the agricultural stabilization board to continue the present levels of price support for the dairy industry during the period May 1, 1960 to April 30, 1961.
The price support for butter during the dairy year May 1, 1960 to April 30, 1961 will be 64 cents per pound for Canada first grade creamery butter scoring 40-93, basis delivery Montreal, with appropriate price differentials for other grades and qualities.
The price support for Ontario cheese, Canada first grade waxed, f.o.b. warehouse, will be 32 cents per pound; and for Quebec cheese, Canada first grade waxed, basis delivery Montreal, 31J cents per pound. In addition, 25 cents per 100 pounds will continue to be paid for whole milk delivered for manufacturing purposes, exclusive of milk from producers who sell a portion of their milk in the fluid, bottled milk market.
During 1959 butter production totalled 324 million pounds, 20 million pounds in excess of the consumption of 304 million pounds, and total stocks of butter as of May 1 will approach 75 million pounds. In view of the potential surplus of butter the agricultural stabilization board is also being authorized to purchase some quantities of whole milk powder as a means of reducing butter production and thereby bring production into a more realistic relationship with consumption. Production of whole milk powder will divert milk from the manufacture of butter and skim milk powder. The total quantity of whole milk powder that will be purchased will depend on the trend of butter production during the year.
The agricultural stabilization board will not purchase any skim milk powder, but the purchase of whole milk powder will not only reduce the potential supply of butter, but will at the same time reduce the amount of skim milk powder manufactured. Ten pounds of whole milk powder is equivalent to approximately 3 pounds of butter and 7.5 pounds of skim milk powder.
During the past two years there has been a progressive decline in butter consumption in

1.	Are the basic costs of hospital treatment in a province participating in the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act deductible from income for federal income tax purposes?
2.	If so, to what extent?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answers to these two questions are rather involved and technical and contain legal terms. I could read them, but with the consent of the house I would ask that they be printed in Hansard rather than attempt to read them at this time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the house unanimously agree that the answers should be printed without being read?

Agreed.
[Editor's note: the answers referred to above are as follows:]
1.	Where, pursuant to section 3 of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, any agreement entered into by and between a province of Canada and the Minister of National Health and Welfare provides for the payment by Canada to that province of contributions in respect of the basic costs of insured hospital services or treatment incurred by the province, the said basic costs of hospital treatment are not ordinarily deductible for purposes of federal income tax. In the majority of instances the participant is not liable to pay for treatment received or, if he is, he is entitled to reimbursement under the provincial plan. In neither case would the expense incurred be deductible for purposes of federal income tax.
2.	Where, however, in any such province as above indicated, additional costs for hospital treatment to cover the difference between the basic costs as prescribed by provincial law (e.g. standard ward care) and,

for instance, the cost of semi-private or private ward care, have been incurred and paid by the taxpayer or reimbursed to him pursuant to the provisions of any other hospital treatment plan, the additional costs so incurred are, subject to the provisions of section 27(l)(c) of the Income Tax Act, deductible for the purposes of federal income tax.
Moreover, hospital expenses incurred in the province by a taxpayer who is not a participant in the plan would also be deductible, subject to the provisions of section 27(l)(c) of the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, last week, as the hon. member knows, I was in New York looking into this matter at the request of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The United Nations scientific committee on radiation has been authorized to send a letter to member nations requesting those nations to forward samples of food, air, soil and water to various nations which have offered facilities to analyse these samples with a view to ascertaining their radioactive content. A number of countries have volunteered to the United Nations scientific committee on radiation to analyse these samples, Canada, of course, being one of the first.
There have been some slight delays in the United Nations scientific committee sending the letter, but these delays were largely unavoidable as the contents of the letter proposed to be circularized had to be submitted to the specialized agencies of the United Nations such as the world health organization, the international atomic energy agency and the like. As a result the letter was circularized to all member nations last Friday, and there should be no additional delay. I would point out that most of the delays were unavoidable, and I should like to add at this time that the co-operation of Dr. Ralph Bunche, who is in charge of the operation at the United Nations, is certainly much appreciated by the Canadian government.

subsubtopic: REPORTED WESTERN REJECTION OF RUSSIAN PROPOSAL ON NUCLEAR WEAPONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Prime Minister, and I apologize for the very short notice I was able to give him. In view of the western delegates' rejection of a Soviet proposal on Monday last in Geneva that the nuclear powers should pledge not to be the first to use nuclear weapons, and in view of the expressed opposition of the Pentagon in the United States to the Soviet proposal, would the Prime Minister

inform the house whether the Canadian decision was influenced by the United States point of view?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REPORTED WESTERN REJECTION OF RUSSIAN PROPOSAL ON NUCLEAR WEAPONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member said in his opening words, no notice was given of this question except after the opening of the house. However, I have been able to secure an answer.
The hon. gentleman has prefaced his question with a misleading suggestion. There has been no separate Soviet proposal in the current negotiations along the lines suggested by him. What happened was that in response to western probing the Soviet representative offered to rearrange the original Khrushchev plan so as to give earlier priority to a proposed pledge respecting the use of nuclear weapons. This proposed rearrangement has not altered the western five-power judgment that the Khrushchev plan as a whole is unacceptable as the sole basis for negotiation.
The stand taken is an agreed western position which does not detract in any way from the unchanged Canadian desire for agreement on early measures of nuclear disarmament under appropriate safeguards. What has happened is in accordance with an agreed western plan to the end that measures leading to disarmament may be secured.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance will excuse me if I do not discuss the budget speech he made the other evening, or if I do not comment


on the very flamboyant and inaccurate speech which he made yesterday. I desire to speak about another subject which is of paramount importance. I shall try to deal with this subject calmly and quietly, leaving aside all considerations of a political nature.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That will be something new.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall try to deal exclusively with the judicial, technical and other aspects of the problem. The facts which I shall give I believe to be true. They were obtained in part from official documents tabled in this house, in part from answers to questions, in part from personal checks which I have made, and in part from reliable information, information so reliable that I could not, as a member of parliament, refrain from bringing it to the attention of the house. If I am inaccurate or incorrect or unfair in my assessment of the situation I am sure the ministers involved will put me right. If I am correct, I hope immediate action will be taken. I hope the ministers will do me the courtesy of hearing me out and making their comments after mine, since both the ministers have been advised of my intention to raise this matter.
I want to discuss Autair Helicopter Services Limited, a corporation which has been in existence in Canada since June, 1957 only. It has little or no experience in the field of heavier helicopter equipment. It was given a licence to operate the S-55 Sikorsky type helicopter contrary to the ruling of the air transport board and against its decision, after having defied its authority. It now holds an important contract to do helicopter work in northern Canada on the polar continental shelf, where men and equipment will have to be moved under difficult and trying circumstances.
What are the facts? On January 25, 1958 an application was made by Autair Helicopter Services Limited to operate (a) a class 4 charter commercial air service, and (b) a class 7 specialty commercial air service restricted to the operation of single helicopters of the Bell-47 and Sikorsky-51 types from a base at St. Eugene in the province of Ontario. The air transport board held a public hearing on this application in Montreal on May 16, 1958. Although it is the practice of the board to move quickly on these applications, it withheld its decision during the latter part of May, all of June and a large part of July, presumably because a change of policy was under consideration by the government.
It is well known, however, what the views of the board were. It was felt that there were enough helicopters in Canada to satisfy the demand. There was no additional helicopter

service needed in Canada, according to the evidence; and upon the evidence adduced at the hearing it is reasonable to believe and conclude that the board would have turned down the application.
On July 14, 1958, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver South, the Minister of Transport announced the decontrol of group C, or the opening up to competition of non-scheduled commercial air services involving the use of small, light aircraft and helicopters. He stated, as reported on page 2207 of Hansard for that date, as follows:
-the government has accordingly decided that it would be in the public interest that licences for air services using only this small type of aircraft be granted freely on request.
On July 18, 1958, exactly four days after the minister announced this change of policy in the house and pursuant to this policy the air transport board by decision serial No. 1111 gave approval to Autair to operate a class 4 charter commercial air service and a class 7 specialty commercial air service from a base at St. Eugene, Ontario, restricted to the operation of single helicopters of the Bell-47 and Sikorsky-51 types.
On November 17, 1958, by air transport board decision serial No. 1198, approval was given to (1) amend licence No. A.T.B. 887/58 (H) to authorize the operation of the additional class 7 recreational flying specialty and (2) for a licence to operate at Quebec city and Montreal a class 4 charter commercial air service and a class 7 specialty commercial air service, restricted to the operation of single engine helicopters of the Bell-47 and Sikorsky-51 types.
On November 26, 1958 an application was made by Autair for the removal of the restrictions to operate single engine helicopters and for permission to operate the heavier and larger type equipment known as the Sikorsky S-55. On June 1, 1959 this application was denied by the air transport board under decision serial No. 1275 on the following grounds:
(a)	That Autair was directed to advertise its request in accordance with board procedure but had failed to do so.
(b)	That Autair file with the board proof of financial responsibility which it refused to do.
(c)	That Autair give to the board certain information requested in letter from the board dated February 4, 1959 which it also refused to do.
(d)	That Autair has consistently refused to provide the board with the information requested and continues so to do.
(e)	In these circumstances the board must judge the request for the removal of the
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier restrictions in the light of the evidence adduced in Montreal on May 16, 1958.
(f)	The board is not satisfied that it would be in the public interest to authorize the applicant to operate with larger aircraft than those permitted under licence A.T.B. 887/58 (H) and the licensee's request is denied.
This decision was appealed to the minister and the minister allowed the appeal on August 20, 1959, as he indicated in his answer to my starred question this morning. The minister stated that in his opinion decision serial No. 1275 should be set aside and the board should issue a licence to the applicant to operate the services requested with no restrictions as to the size of the aircraft in such service. On September 1, 1959 the board complied with the request.
My contention is that the minister ought not to have interfered with the decision of the board, for the following reasons. First, the board in denying the application was exercising a judicial function, and the minister ought not to have interfered with the board in what was regarded by them, I am sure, as a judicial matter based upon the evidence adduced at the hearing in Montreal. That is borne out, too, by the fact that when the Aeronautics Act was introduced in this house it was clearly stated that so far as judicial matters were concerned there should be no interference in the decisions of the board. The minister ought not to have interfered with the decision of the board, in my opinion, because Autair had categorically refused to advertise its application in accordance with board procedure and refused to furnish proof of financial responsibility as required by the board. Autair still continues to ignore the judgment of the board in that respect. That is my second reason for thinking the minister ought not to have interfered.
My third contention is that Autair had been operating helicopters commercially without a licence, according to information in my possession, in contravention of the Aeronautics Act prior to July 18, 1958. With respect to the specific period from April to July 18, here are the facts. Three helicopters operated on a contract for the Quebec government, which contract began in June, 1958. One helicopter operated for a private company under a contract which began on June 4, 1958. Still another helicopter operated for another department of the Quebec government under a contract beginning April 9, 1958, all in contravention and in violation of the Aeronautics Act.
The president of Autair in his evidence before the air transport board stated that these helicopter services were operating on a demonstration basis only, and that no
3196	KOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier remuneration was being received for these flights. However, these flights were expensive. The monthly tariff for work of this kind is I am informed $4,500, but he flew for nothing. A compilation of the cost of these flights indicates that three helicopters operated from June, 1958 to July 18, 1958, equalling one and one quarter months or three and three quarter aircraft months. One helicopter operated between June 4 and July 18, 1958, equalling one and one half months or one and one half aircraft months. One helicopter operated between April 9 and July 18, 1958, equalling three and one quarter months or three and one quarter aircraft months. This equals eight and one half aircraft months at $4,500, a total of $38,225. Autair therefore flew five aircraft without charge for which he would be entitled to receive the sum of $38,225 prior to obtaining his licence in July of 1958. Thereafter, I am informed, he increased his tariff from $4,500 to $6,000 per month so as to recapture the loss encountered prior to obtaining the licence.
A fourth reason why the minister ought not to have granted the appeal is because of the safety factor. Autair is not an experienced helicopter operator. At pages 14 and 15 of the evidence given before the board the president of the company stated that he had 35 hours of helicopter time. That has since been increased to 50 or 60 hours, I am advised. Also, as found at page 79 of the evidence, it was proved at the time of the hearing that at least one of the S-51 helicopters had outstanding liens against it, which information had been filed with the Department of Transport by the United States owner of the equipment.
The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys has granted a contract to Autair for helicopter services in northern Canada, namely on the continental polar shelf. The date of commencement of this contract is imminent, if it has not already started. It is a most important contract, located as it is on the northwest side of the Queen Elizabeth islands. Furthermore, this is extremely dangerous work. It is to move supplies and persons, including surgeons and geologists, to that area. Great care should be taken to see that lives are protected. Helicopter operations are delicate and experience means a lot. Few operators in this country have the experience required to fulfil a job of this nature.
I believe the air transport board, the body charged with the responsibility of determining these technical matters under the Aeronautics Act, thought that in the public interest they should not grant these people a licence. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys apparently thought otherwise, and has given them a contract.


The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys in my opinion ought not to have recommended the contract to Autair for work on the polar shelf for the following reasons. A careful analysis of the sessional paper which the minister tabled in the house, No. 235 tabled on March 25, 1960, indicates that the tariff filed by Autair was not the lowest. In December, 1959 the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys informed five companies, Autair, Kenting, Okanagan, Pacific and Spartan that the department would require one Sikorsky S-55 helicopter and two Bell 47-G helicopters for their polar shelf program during the summer of 1960. The requirements were set out and the companies were requested to advise the department if they were interested and to enclose with their replies copies of their relevant tariffs as filed with the air transport board. All five companies did so signify and sent copies of their tariffs. Pacific was eliminated because it did not operate the S-55 type of helicopter. Strangely enough Autair was not so eliminated, although it had not operated S-55 helicopters and did not own any such equipment.
On February 9, 1960 Autair, I am informed on reliable information, was told by the departmental officers of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys that Okanagan had the lowest tariff and that a decision had been made the day before February 8, to give the contract to Okanagan because of their greater experience and stable record. As a matter of fact, Okanagan were given a letter of intent from the department covering the operation.
The next day, February 10, Autair filed a new tariff with the air transport board which brought their rates down from the highest of the four companies to the following, as set out in the return tabled by the minister, and which upon examination indicates, first, that on the minimum rates they were tied with Okanagan and Spartan; second, that on the 50 hours of operation per month they were a little higher than Okanagan and Spartan but lower than Kenting; and third, that on the 100 hours of operation per month they were slightly lower than Okanagan and Spartan.
A submission was then prepared at the request of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys recommending the contract to be given to Autair as the company with the lowest rates. This was done in spite of the fact that Autair possessed no S-55 helicopters; had never operated them; had never operated in the Arctic at all; had rates, even under its new tariff, that were the same as or higher than its competitors except when flying over

100 hours per month per machine, a rather unlikely figure under extreme Arctic weather conditions. This was done under the minister's direction, and Autair was given the contract on the basis of a tariff filed the day after all four companies had been told the decision was made.
Autair thus knew exactly the rates they had to beat, and since none of the other companies could know that the minister had changed the award these other competitors had no opportunity to file competitive tariffs. Thus the contract was handed by the minister to Autair without any chance of interference by the other companies.
The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys ought to have been more careful in granting a contract to be carried out in that strategic area of Canada for another reason. At this stage I would like to put on record information which has already been made public by the United States magazine Newsweek, which information to my knowledge has not been contradicted. Here is what is said in the issue of January 30, 1950 at page 33, in an article entitled "How Pan Am plane parts were smuggled behind the Iron Curtain":
Newsweek has uncovered a striking example of how desperately the satellite states still are trying to open a chink in this American economic iron curtain. The state department suspected that Czechoslovakia had been obtaining essential American airplane engines and parts for its fleet of DC-3s. And last week the state department discovered to its astonishment that some illegal shipments had originally been purchased from Pan American World Airways-apparently the victim of an extraordinary case of international doubledealing. Edward Weintal, Newsweek diplomatic correspondent here gives the full story.
Mr. Speaker, because of time I can only quote a part of this story. I continue:
For some time the operations of the Czechoslovak air lines have been under constant scrutiny of various agencies of the United States government. The line is believed to be operating under Moscow's orders and used for transporting Cominform agents ...
Virtually all planes of the Czech line are American DC-3s. All western European governments have been warned by the state department to be on the lookout for Czech-bound DC-3 engines and parts. But despite these warnings the Czech line did not show any signs of shortages.
Evidence from various sources pointed to Belgium as the origin of American engines and spare parts for the Czechoslovak air lines. Howard Railey, the state department's aviation expert normally stationed in Paris, was ordered to Brussels. Railey's preliminary survey confirmed the state department's suspicions. The Belgium government was asked to investigate and urged to tighten up its own export controls. But before the Belgium government had a chance to comply, Railey found that some supplies for the Czechs were being purchased from Pan American World Airways by an unknown concern going by the name of Global Aviation of New York.
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
I now pass over a number of paragraphs because it is not possible to read all this, article; I read only the pertinent parts.
Little is known about the Global Aviation Co. It is believed to be a partnership made up of D. W. Connor-
Who incidentally is the president of Autair, which has received this contract to work on the polar continental shelf.
-a former Canadian air force pilot, and E. F. O'Mara, a United States-born naturalized Canadian, citizen.

Having said that, I would add that these statements are of a most serious nature. They are made in a reputable magazine. I have nomeans of knowing whether they are true or not, but the public is entitled to know before this company is given a government contract and a licence to operate. Did the air transport board know about this? If it did, this may be one of the reasons why it turned down the application. The government should not have given a contract until it had fully investigated the story.
Now let me quote from the evidence which the Minister of Transport was good enough to table in this house in answer to my request. This man D. W. Connor, president of Autair Helicopter Services Limited, was examined before the air transport board in Montreal on May 16, 1958 on application for a licence. At page 14 of the evidence he was asked:
Q. How many hours have you?
A. About 35 . ..
Q. You have never operated a helicopter company prior to this?
A. Prior to last year, no.
Q. You say you are a resident of Westmount. When did you return to Canada?
A. In December of last year.
That would be 1957.
Q. Prior to that time you had been living in England?
A. Yes.
Q. Since 1948?
A. No. I lived in Switzerland until 1952.
Q. From the time of your discharge from the R.C.A.F. you have lived in Switzerland and then in England?
A. England, Switzerland and England, in that order, if you want to be exact.
Q. The air engine service group commenced operations in 1952?
A. Yes.
Q. Prior to that you said "We operated a delivery service for aircraft''. Who do you mean by "we"?
A. The Connair Corporation.

The Budget-Mr. Comtois
Q. Were you associated with any other companies?
A. Yes. I was at that time also president of Global Aviation.
Q. What did Global Aviation do?
A. It ferried and delivered airplanes around the world.
Q. Did it buy and sell airplanes at all?
A. It did.
Q. All over the world?
A. In certain countries.
Q. To what countries did Global Aviation deliver airplanes and equipment?
A. You tax my memory after ten years, and it seems quite irrelevant, but South America, South Africa, Sweden, Norway, Belgium, Egypt, certainly Pakistan and Yugoslavia; generally anywhere you .could find a market for the airplanes.
Q. That is commercial business?
A. Yes.
Can anyone believe that the president of this company would have mentioned Pakistan, Egypt, South America, Yugoslavia, and not have remembered the story in Newsweek about Czechoslovakia? This is a most serious matter. I cannot believe that either of the ministers concerned had read this story in Newsweek or the evidence before the board. That is why I consider it my duty to bring the matter before the house. Much of it, if not all, is already known in the aviation industry, and much of it has already been referred to in the press. If these statements which I have brought before the house are accurate, immediate action should be taken by the government, and in any case this company should not be allowed to proceed with this work until a thorough investigation has been made.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in case I should have misled the house in my reply to the hon. member for Trinity with regard to the Bomarc missile, may I say that at six minutes past twelve today I received information that a Bomarc B had been fired from Eglin field and that it was completely successful. I did not have that information when I was replying to the hon. member.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF SUCCESSFUL FIRING
speechtext:
In view of the fact that the house allowed the minister to make this statement, I hope I shall be permitted to say that we on this side are pleased that at least one of these Bomarc missiles has proved successful. I should like to add, however, that it does not establish our confidence


in this missile by one iota. We still feel that for Canada to continue the installation of this missile system is a complete waste of the taxpayers' money and that, further, such pressure as this country is putting on the United States is, in addition to our own money, wasting $250 million of the United States taxpayers' funds. So we urge the minister not to be too reassured by this single example of success by this Bomarc, and suggest that he should consider the immediate cancellation of the whole system on the ground that it is of no further military value.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REPORT OF SUCCESSFUL FIRING
speechtext: If the Minister of Transport would defer for a moment I will hear the hon. member for Port Arthur commenting on the statement which has been made.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: REPORT OF SUCCESSFUL FIRING
speechtext: I should like to congratulate the minister on his guess -because it has been a guess-and I also wish to agree with the statement made by the hon. member for Trinity. Although this firing has been successful, we are not in agreement that Canada should pursue the installation of the Bomarc defence system even though one test has been successful-and on that we congratulate the minister.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REPORT OF SUCCESSFUL FIRING
speechtext: May I call attention to the fact that I recognized the hon. member for Port Arthur, but it turned out to be the hon. member for Timiskaming. The rules require hon. members to rise in their own places. The same applies to the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) who has been contributing to the debate from a seat not his own.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) that Mr. Speaker now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I intend to speak very briefly, because there is nothing very much in the speech made by the hon. member for Laurier which requires a reply. I think the hon. gentleman's speech could best be termed much ado about nothing. The impression had been given that this was going to be an earth-shattering speech, but as far as I can see it brought forth nothing which had not already been made known by myself on several occasions, and in particular, when I announced the introduction of this new policy last fall.
The hon. member asked me specifically about the part played by my own department. He asked me why I, as minister, had

overridden a decision of the air transport board regarding the Autair application. The air transport board had been operating under a policy laid down by the former government, a policy which favoured monopoly, and which denied competition. This present government, as I have said on several occasions, believes that it has a responsibility, not only to the aircraft industry but also to the users of air services. This government believes that competition among charter air services leads to the provision of better and cheaper services to the public, and also serves as a healthy stimulant to the industry itself.
It was for that reason that I, on behalf of this government, introduced a freeing-up with respect to the granting of licences in the charter field. I made it very clear that I did so because it was the basic belief of the government that this would be a good thing for the industry, and no detriment; that in fact it would stimulate the provision of more of these services for the public. That, and that alone, was the reason I overrode the decision of the air transport board.
In this case, when the application was denied, it was denied in conformity with the policy imposed upon the board by the former government, a policy with which, in this regard, the present government does not agree. That is the reason the application was granted, and that is the reason we are now operating under a much freer system of granting licences, one which we believe will be of benefit to the industry itself.
I think that is all I have to deal with in connection with my own department and the air transport board. I am sure the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys will deal more than adequately with matters which relate to the operations of his department.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Would he say whether, when he overrode the decision of the air transport board, he was aware of the fact that this company had not complied, as the hon. member for Laurier said, with the request of the board to provide statements of financial responsibility and other information which the law requires any company to provide?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1 was aware of that and the impression I had of that requirement was simply that the provision of charter air services is in no way different from the provision of so many other services provided by other industries to users in this country. Under the free democratic system, which we fought several world wars to preserve, a man has the right to enter business and lose his shirt, if he wants to, and nobody stops him doing it. If I want to go into business, in any
The Budget-Mr. Comtois line of business at all in this country, I can do so. Before going into business I do not have to prove that I have a certain financial stability. I have the right-and we jealously maintain that right in a democracy such as this-to go into business, and if I fail it is my own sorrow. For that reason the requirement referred to seemed a ridiculous requirement in these particular cases, where the service provided is not that of a scheduled air service, which is a definite service to the public. This is a charter service where those providing the service do so under no compulsion, and before contracting to provide a service they are satisfied that the terms under which they will be providing that service are satisfactory to them.
For that reason I felt that the requirement under which the board was operating in this particular regard was one which I did not agree with and, therefore, I considered it did not affect me in any way in granting this licence.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am disposed to regard the matter before the house, raised by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), as a separate subject, and therefore I would recognize those who wish to speak on that subject in priority to others. The minister wishes to speak on the subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Are there any other members who wish to speak on this subject. I may be mistaken in the procedure I am following, but it is my view that when the motion before the house is that I leave the chair, with no amendment outstanding, we are really under grievance procedure as we would be on a motion for the Speaker to leave the chair to go into committee of supply. That, I think, is the reason why the rule calls for a vote before the maximum time limit of the debate is reached. If hon. members agree with me on that I will follow that course for the remainder of this debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Comtois (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just wrote down a few notes during the speech made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), who was kind enough, this morning, to notify me of his intention of dealing with the matter of a contract awarded to Autair Helicopter Services Limited.
The hon. member for Laurier has an axe to grind. That is obvious. And I even wonder whether his intervention today, and the grievances L voiced, are not perhaps related to the fact that one of the top officials of

The Budget-Mr. Comtois Okanagan Helicopters is the former election organizer for ex-minister Sinclair. There might be some connection between the two circumstances. However, I would not like to vouch for it, because I have no information to that effect. If I am mistaken, so much the better.
The hon. member for Laurier, it seems, wants to raise a storm in a tea cup. He imagines there has been a scandal, that there were false representations, in other words something irregular in the contract awarded to Autair Helicopter Services Limited. My department has nothing whatsoever to do with licences or prices submitted to the transport commission. That is not our job. It is the responsibility of the Department of Transport, and the minister replied to that. He said what he had to say with regard to the duties of his department.
With regard to matters that concern us, we were called upon to award a contract in the north for a survey and inspection expedition in the Arctic. We asked companies having the required qualifications to submit prices. We did not call for tenders because, as I had the opportunity to say in reply to a question asked in this house, prices are established in advance by the transport commission, and the duty of my officials is to determine the best possible price so as not to pay more than required, that is, to obtain the most economic price to the department, to the government and to the whole country. That is what we did. There was no intention, as stated by the hon. member for Laurier, of awarding the contract to the Okanagan Helicopters Company. That letter was never sent, so I am informed by my department. Therefore, when the hon. member states that the letter was sent, I think he was misinformed.
Second, I asked that the tenders sent in by the various companies be examined, and that the matter be fully considered, always in keeping with the economic aspect of the contract. It was established that for a hundred hours of flight a month by a Bell-47 G the Renting Helicopters Limited submitted a price of $97,560, whereas the Autair Helicopters Services Limited, quoted $93,600, the Spartan Air Services Limited, $91,200 and the Okanagan Helicopters Limited, also $91,200.
Therefore, as far as that part of the contract was concerned, the price quoted by Autair Helicopters for a Bell-47 G plane was of course, not the lowest. However, with

regard to the S 55 plane, the Autair Helicopters Company had asked for an amount of $109,200 whereas the Okanagan Helicopters Limited, the Spartan Air Services Limited as well as the Renting Helicopters Limited were quoting $115,200. Therefore, the Autair Helicopters Co. had submitted the most favourable price, that is, $109,200. When awarding contracts, the department has to consider the total cost of the expedition, and this was done.
We acted in a perfectly proper way. I wanted to avoid any unfairness.
Mr. Speaker, I must point out that I am totally opposed to monopolies, and I can say quite frankly that having gone over the file, I found that Okanagan Helicopters Limited had always got the contracts, on the basis that it had a monopoly on experience. Thus the government was at the mercy of a firm which claimed to be alone in having the required experience in the north-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are three others.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if there are three others, one of them is the Autair Helicopter Services Limited. It has as much experience as any other, because it is a matter of piloting, and if the pilots of that firm have experience in the north, they are just as qualified as those of Okanagan Helicopters Limited or of any other firm. That type of experience can be compared to driving experience; a good driver avoids the hazards of the road.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let him have it, Mr. Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The pilots of Autair Helicopter Services are as qualified as those of Okanagan Helicopters Limited, of Spartan Air Services Limited or of Renting Helicopters Limited.
We took every proper precaution, and decided to grant the contraot to Autair Helicopter Services. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I might say that I do not know the president of that firm. I had no confession certificate to expect from him.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He was not your organizer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not gone into the matter that far; I am not interested in the personal life of company presidents. I do not care whether he had been in some other country, across the border or even abroad. We are dealing with the directors of the company and we are satisfied that we will get excellent service.

We followed the standard practice and the lowest tender was accepted. That is the course my departmental officials decided to follow. No other consideration than the lowest tender entered into the award of the contract to Autair Helicopter Services Limited.
I am glad that this course was followed, even if the president of that company is not one of the friends of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), nor a friend of the hon. members opposite. I did not ask the president about his political affiliations. I do not know what they are. But now the Okanagan Helicopters Limited will not be the only company with experience in the north.
The pilots of Autair Helicopter Services Limited acquired experience on the D.E.W. line, and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, there is not much difference between the D.E.W. line and the areas where those aircraft will fly. I believe that to get Arctic experience you always have to start somewhere and if, each year, we keep saying that we must carry on only with people who have previously worked in the area we might just as well not call for tenders from any one and tell the Okanagan company-
It had been a Liberal monopoly.

- "You have the monopoly, so go ahead." Mr. Speaker, I felt we had to be fair to everybody and that we should consider the tenders in the light of the projects we had in mind. Everything has been done on the up-and-up and there is nothing further I can say on the subject.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the subject raised by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) simply in reply to what has been said by the two ministers who have spoken. I do think that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) would have been well advised to follow the example of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) who treated this subject seriously, dealt with it on its merits and did not make unworthy insinuations about there being any political matters involved here.
Oh, oh.
Does the truth hurt?

I might also draw hon. members' attention to the fact that when
The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill the two ministers were speaking we listened to them with politeness and without interruption.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman did last night?
It seems to me that on a matter as grave as this, hon. gentlemen on the back benches would be well advised to speak when their turn comes.

We will.
Another hon. Member: What did you do last night?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I trust hon. members will observe the rule against interruption while the hon. member has the floor.

I have no new argument, Mr. Speaker, but I want to debate what has already been raised by my hon. friend from Laurier. The Minister of Transport said that when he overruled the air transport board he thought that these conditions having to do with financial responsibility and capacity to perform, about which I asked him a question, were unimportant, and that anyone in this free country was perfectly entitled to enter freely into any kind of business. Of course, that is not true. One cannot enter into the railway business without getting a charter from parliament or from a provincial legislature. I am also reliably informed that one cannot go into the taxi business in most large municipalities without satisfying a board of one's financial competence and one's capacity, and in many cases the supply is limited so that the public will have some assurance of the capacity of the operators and also some assurance that the people who are operating the taxis are reliable members of society. One could go on to give many other examples both in the federal and provincial fields and under governments of every political complexion.

On a question of privilege, may I correct a misapprehension? I was not dealing with the ability to operate; I was simply dealing with the amount of finances behind the company. With respect to ability to operate, my department has very strict safety regulations, and any company that cannot comply at all times with these safety regulations is not allowed to fly.

I am very glad that the minister has made that correction because I do not want to be unfair in any way about this matter. But I will draw the minister's attention to the fact that the hon, member

The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill for Laurier made certain very precise statements on this point. He said that this company, at the time the minister removed the restriction against it with respect to the use of large helicopters, did not own any large helicopters at all. He went on to say that Autair did not own any large helicopters at the time they were asked by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to bid on this business.

Would the hon. member permit a question? I should like to ask him how a company could ever operate with large helicopters before having obtained a licence? Why in the world would they ever buy these large helicopters until they had obtained a licence to operate such large helicopters? Otherwise they would simply have a lot of white elephants on their hands which they could not use.

If the minister had listened carefully to the hon. member for Laurier I think he would have had the answer to that question. This company does seem to have had an unenviable record of operating small helicopters for some considerable time without any licence on the pretense that they were operating them for demonstration purposes, but at the same time taking good care to recoup themselves for those operations later, if my hon. friend was correctly informed, from the government of Quebec. It does not necessarily have to be the case, but I think there is something in the contention of the Minister of Transport that perhaps this company would not have acquired helicopters until it was assured that it would have a licence to operate.
That does not at all dispose of the other statement by my hon. friend, namely that in 1960, many months after the minister had quashed the decision of the board, this company still had no large helicopters when it and these other four companies were invited to bid on this survey work in the north. That is what my hon. friend alleged, and he also stated that one of these companies, Pacific, I believe, was ruled out of the bidding because it did not own any large helicopters. I think the house and the country are entitled to know why Pacific was ruled out and Autair, in exactly the same circumstances with no large helicopters, was not ruled out. They had had a licence for some time but they had no large helicopters. That is quite serious.
Moreover, it was shown in the evidence before the board, which my hon. friend read, that this company had very little experience in operating small helicopters and did not even own a large helicopter. Yet they were preferred over three experienced operators


qualified in every way to do this work. It does seem to me that in this contract there was no question of private enterprise. Maybe if some private company was going to hire Autair there perhaps would not be the same concern about the matter. I say "perhaps"; I am not sure about that. But what is the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys going to do? He is going to send these people up to the polar shelf. He is going to send public servants in these aircraft and endanger their lives. Their lives will be endangered no matter who does the work because those of us who have had some experience of travelling in helicopters know that this is not quite the safest form of travel. It does seem to me, that before the minister allows this to happen, allows the lives of these public servants to be in danger, in the light of what my hon. friend from Laurier has placed before the minister there should be the fullest investigation of every allegation put forward this morning. No one should make light of these allegations.
There may be nothing in this story in Newsweek. It may have no foundation whatever. My hon. friend from Laurier made it very clear he did not know whether or not it was true. We all know that this is a very reputable publication. We all know that the diplomatic correspondent would not just publish gossip and hearsay. This magazine is subject to the libel laws and other laws of that kind in the United States. It does seem to me that if the two ministers, or either of them, did not know about these statements beforehand they should now be very hesitant about sending this company, in the face of that story, up to the Arctic, right on the edge of the iron curtain. They would be sending someone who, according to this reputable United States publication, at one time was supposed to have been smuggling aircraft parts behind the iron curtain.
I do not believe we should prejudge this case; that is the last thing we would ask. But we think it should be investigated and cleared up. The minister should remember what happened in this house earlier today in connection with this unfortunate woman in British Columbia who is going to be deported from this country apparently merely because of a suspicion she may be a danger to the security of the country. I am not questioning that at this moment. I am saying when we take that kind of precaution in that case, surely it is not asking anything excessive when my hon. friend from Laurier, as he did in his closing words, requested the members of the government to clear this thing up and clear it up without any equivocation, before we let a company headed by a

man against whom allegations of that kind were made in a reputable United States journal undertake this kind of work on the polar shelf.
Then, there is one other statement with which the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys did not deal. I refer to the very serious statement made by my hon. friend from Laurier. The hon. member says he is informed-he did not say that he knew but that he was reliably informed-that five bids were submitted originally. One was disallowed and the other four were considered. A decision was reached by the department in favour of one of those companies and unfavourable to Autair, and then a change was made and Autair was allowed to make a second submission while the other companies apparently were not. I do not know anything about whether or not that is true. I have not the faintest idea whether or not it is true because I have made no personal investigation into this matter at all. I listened to the hon. member for Laurier as he was speaking, and I tried to listen very attentively. I think that is what he said. I believe, that is a point that should be cleared up, and cleared up seriously, not brushed off with a suggestion there are some petty politics in this matter.
It seems to me that these are the five points. First, this company has refused to demonstrate its financial worthiness to the air transport board. Is it financially competent to carry out a contract with the government of Canada? Surely the minister or the treasury board would satisfy themselves about that. When we ask a contractor to build a small post office in the maritime provinces, as my hon. friend from Levis (Mr. Bourget) knows, we satisfy ourselves he is financially competent to do it. According to the evidence before the board, this operator refused to satisfy them of his financial competence, refused to answer their questions, and to the best of our knowledge that has never been cleared up. Yet he has been given a contract which was refused to other companies with demonstrated financial competence.
Then there is the question of safety, the fact that this company has never operated one of these large helicopters. This company is preferred over other companies to carry scientists and other public servants into this area. Then there is the very grave question of national security. It seems to me before this contract proceeds these matters should be cleared up and cleared up to public satisfaction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should like to raise a point of order, and I do so because of the
The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill doubt which Your Honour expressed as to the correctness of the procedure which we have been adopting. I ask that this procedure should not be considered a precedent until Your Honour has had an opportunity to give mature consideration to it.
It seems to me when the house has before it a motion to resolve itself into committee of ways and means, the budget, that the procedure on supply motions in respect of grievances is not appropriate thereto. I venture to submit to Your Honour that it is incongruous on the eighth day of the budget debate that any hon. member should be able to raise a subject which is totally unrelated to the budget and should thereby preclude discussion of the budget itself. It is true that under the ordinary motion for the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means, under citation 234, on Monday and Tuesday, it is possible for any member to ask for the redress of any grievance. I suggest, however, that does not apply where the situation is as set forth in standing order 58, subsection 2, which provides for the debate on the motion for the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means, the budget. My submission is that this motion related as it is to the budget is different from the ordinary motion which is referred to in citation 234.
I rise only to speak at this time so that this procedure will not be considered as a precedent before Your Honour has had an opportunity to give mature consideration to the problem.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to speak to the point of order, if I may.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps we might call it one o'clock. Will the hon. member be here after the adjournment?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at two o'clock.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to argue this point of order at any length because I do not think I am too much in disagreement with the hon. member who raised it. The only purpose of my rising on the point of order is to make it quite clear to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that I had a perfect right to discuss anything that I felt like discussing on the budget because, after all, the letting of a contract and the expenditure of public moneys comes entirely within the budget. Whether it is a specific

The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill matter or a general matter, I do not think makes any difference. That was really the only purpose of my rising.
On the other hand, if I may add this, it may well be that because of the right I feel I have and because of the point that has been raised by the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Bell) Your Honour may feel that this is a point to which Your Honour should .give consideration and if Your Honour did feel that way certainly I would be quite happy to abide by that decision.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not disagree with the hon. gentleman's right to raise the particular issue he did. My point of order relates only to the question of whether, when the hon. gentleman raises that issue, all debate thereafter on the eighth day shall be confined to the issue which he raised.
My submission is that in a case where it is a motion to go into committee of ways and means, the budget-and that I emphasize- there is not that confinement to the particular grievance that has been raised by a particular hon. gentleman. The hon. member may raise whatever he wishes although I may have some views as to the wisdom of a senior privy councillor doing so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have been trying to be friendly to my hon. friend in not disagreeing with him but the position a senior privy councillor takes is his own decision and should not be reflected upon by the junior hon. member for Carleton.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just one word. When this point was first raised I found it difficult not to agree with the position that had been taken on the other side with regard to the interpretation of the rule. I think there are occasions when we should seek to strengthen our procedures by not being afraid to assert positions that are taken by those who sit opposite. This may be one of those occasions.
My submission is that if there has been a violation of the rules the violation was not on this side. The violation would consist in the participation by two ministers, one after the other, without observing the traditional practice of this house of providing for alternations between the various parties.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I take full responsibility for the order in which hon. members spoke in this matter. Perhaps I was presuming too much on my own authority in suggesting the procedure we followed today which was not the procedure followed last year, the year before or in fact since the rule was amended in 1955.

I have given some thought to the question of what happens after the amendment has been disposed of on the motion to go into committee of ways and means, the budget. It struck me-and I think perhaps hon. members who were on the committee which revised the rules may be able to verify this -that the reason the vote was provided for on the seventh day, leaving a full day for further discussion, was to provide on the budget debate an opportunity for a discussion of this kind. A motion of this nature like a supply motion is connected with the voting of moneys for the crown and is preceded by the airing of all the grievances parliament has to air. However, as this debate has been entered upon in the expectation that it would follow the usual pattern I think it would be very imprudent for me to attempt to change horses in midstream and that we should conclude the debate in the way it has been done in the last few years.
Perhaps if and when the committee is set up to consider these matters some thought might be given to the wisdom of the course which I have suggested earlier today because it makes a connected discussion of a grievance possible. It concludes that grievance and another is then entered upon. And then, in supply motions, it gives more members an opportunity to speak than happens when hon. members are speaking at large.
Therefore I quite readily accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) that this matter be given further consideration. There is time for perhaps only two more speeches and unless some other hon. member has something to say on this subject we shall proceed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am impelled to say just a word or two on this point of order by reason of the reference to the committee which revised the rules of the house. I think I am the only hon. member in the chamber at the moment who was a member of the committee which revised the rules which became effective in 1955. That committee sat through three sessions.
I may say that the reason for providing for the votes on the subamendment, the amendment and finally on the main motion on different days was not the reason that you purported to assign to it at all. It was to avoid a situation which had become altogether too common where the debate purported to continue on the submendment and then, when the debate had run its course, there were three votes taken in quick succession on the subamendment, the amendment and finally on the main motion. It was thought in the committee it would be better to space out the votes. It was not done at all, I assure you,

on the part of the committe with any thought that by having provided that the vote on the main motion should come at the conclusion of the seventh day the debate on the eighth day should change its nature. It still continues as part of the debate on the budget. It does not change its character and become assimilable with the normal procedure on a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply or a motion to go into ways and means in which case we would have the normal provision for airing grievances.
I think on the eighth day the house and the debate are in much the same position as at the time of launching the debate originally on the part of the first speaker from the opposition side of the house. He ranges widely, usually over many matters, and then winds up his speech by offering an amendment. I think the amendment and the subamendment now having been disposed of, the debate is in the same position as it was at that time. It is still a debate on the budget and is not a new debate of a different nature, resolving itself simply into a matter of raising individual grievances and exhausting each before another is raised.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I refer to Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 229, which rather bears out the contention raised by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell):
When an amendment for the Speaker's leaving the chair has been negatived, no further amendment can be moved thereto; though general debate on the main question can be maintained by those members who have not exhausted their right to speak to that question.
The other citation which is relevant is citation 234, which rather supports the view I have taken.

Mr. Speaker, may I raise a question of privilege. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
You are being the brass band right now. In a calm voice, the Minister of Finance spoke the first lines of his text in impeccable French. There was another thunderous burst of applause.
That man, Mr. Speaker, had just made a friendly gesture toward the Canadian population which welcomed that expression of understanding on his part. I am saying "Canadian" because the reaction was favourable, not only in Quebec but throughout the country.
Though, unaware of it at the time, the Minister of Finance was replying to a vicious and unfair attack by a C.C.F. member, for whom I have no animosity, but who does not seem to know the province of Quebec at all and who does not seem to wish to know it. That attack came a few days later. The conclusion to be drawn from that, Mr. Speaker, is that we must blame the one who has a sense of responsibility, but forgive the one who has none. Why attack a population which has always worked in co-operation with other provinces, for the greatness and progress of Canada as a whole and in favour of a sound national unity?
Recently, Hon. Antonio Barrette, the premier of Quebec confirmed what I am now saying by expressing the real feeling of the province of Quebec, when he met in Toronto with hon. Mr. Frost, the premier of Ontario and the hon. members of the legislature.
Hon. Mr. Barrette did something which is much more eloquent than any words can say, and I will simply quote what the Globe and Mail of Toronto reported on April 8, 1960:
(Text):
For the first time since confederation the premiers of Ontario and Quebec yesterday stood in the same legislative assembly.
And the pledge of eternal friendship and partnership that was associated with the union of 1867 was enunciated again clearly by Premier Frost and Quebec's Premier Barrette.
Symbolicly the two premiers stood near the Speaker's throne over which is inscribed the date of the first pledge of national unity made 93 years ago.

The Budget-Mr. English
Premier Frost said that it was with a deep sense of honour that the Ontario house greeted the Quebec premier, who represents "our neighbours and partners from the beginning."
"They have always been our good partners, our good friends.. . We ask you, sir, to take back to your people our affectionate regards," said Premier Frost.
Premier Barrette told the legislature that he had intended to speak from notes.
"But I put them aside and very simply speak to you from the bottom of my heart," he said.
"We are partners," he said. "We have always been partners, even when we sometimes thought that we were not. We have fought together... we will remain partners."
Premier Frost said that the challenge of 1867- to build a nation of French and English culture- has been achieved.
And opposition leader Wintermeyer said that the present Canadian challenge is the same as that faced by Macdonald and Laurier. They had fought to build a nation against all economic odds and with a union of two cultures. Today the challenge was to build an even greater nation from many different cultures besides English and French.
(Translation):
Is it not true, Mr. Speaker, that such a gesture deserves to be emphasized, and is it not another proof that all provincial premiers want to show to the country that they want to unite and co-operate in carrying out a wish close to the heart of each and everyone of us? Mr. Speaker, I would like sincerely to congratulate the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) for having addressed a few words in the beginning of his speech in the chamber yesterday in I might add very good French. The hon. member gave an example of what we call real national unity.

Coming back to the Minister of Finance, I should like to quote an article from La Presse for April 1, 1960:
Fleming starts his speech in French.
Though not wearing a blue carnation on his lapel, as he had last year, but smiling broadly, Finance Minister Fleming was greeted in the House of Commons yesterday with thunderous applause.
The applause doubled when, directly in French and without any English preliminary, he opened his speech with these words: "Mr. Speaker, for a third time it is my honour and privilege to present to the house the annual budget". By this, the minister renewed a precedent set by himself in June 1958 when he brought down his first budget. In that year, it was the first time in Canada's history that a minister of finance delivered parts of his budget speech in French. Last year, Mr. Fleming confirmed the precedent by delivering three lengthy parts of his speech in French. This year, he went further and opened his remarks in the language which, as he said, "has so gracefully

adorned the proceedings of this house and holds a secure constitutional position in the Canadian parliament."
Apparently, the opposition is not too satisfied with the budget. That is probably due to the fact that it has too many qualities.
Its first quality is balance. Mr. Fleming has an acute sense of reality, and so far, his judgement has been born out by the facts.
Here is what the Gazette for April 1, 1960 had to say on the subject, and I quote: (Text):
Mr. Fleming has decided that the trends and impulses set in motion by the tax changes for 1959-60 will be sufficient to reach the desired result in 1960-61. This result is, of course, a balanced budget.
(Translation):
This is what we read in La Presse of April 1, 1960:
Observers had unanimously forecast that Mr. Fleming would present a balanced budget. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Finance gave us, as we put it elsewhere, a super-balanced budget, providing a slim margin of $12 million on a budget of $5,892, million, without considering the $600 million or so which the old age security program would cost.
He did not even slightly increase taxes, trusting only in the continuance of the present economic rhythm.
In a serious effort, the minister was able to realize the miracle of foreseeing a surplus while not increasing taxes. The surplus is $12 million.
To balance a budget is one thing. Not to increase taxes and tariffs is even better. But to offer salary increases is just splendid. And that is what the Minister of Finance achieved in his last budget. The people owe him their gratitude, and deserving government employees joyfully welcome such generosity.
The Conservative party does not choose roundabout ways. It attacks in a straightforward manner problems that are sometimes very complex, and obtains results about which each and everyone can marvel and which throw the opposition into the deepest gloom. Now that is what Montreal-Matin of April 1, 1960 said:
Fifty thousand civil servants are benefiting from salary increases. When announcing the decision, Mr. Fleming however warned that the days of "across-the-board increases" were past and that such increases would from now on, be granted after thoroughly considering each category and the functions attached thereto. The increases, averaging about $300 a year, will be granted mainly to clerical and stenographic categories.
The last general salary increase granted to federal civil servants came on May 1st 1957.
The increase, which will be effective tomorrow, will cost some $15 million to the treasury.
Not only do civil servants benefit from the wise Conservative administration, but widows

too can count on improved benefits. It is in time of difficulty that we recognize those who are sincere. The minister wanted to give some protection to this category, and rightly so.
The budget is also an example of shrewd administration. There is no more one-way contribution to the old age pension item. Quite the contrary, it is a period of prosperity. And that is something the opposition cannot get over. You can be sure, Mr. Speaker, that they will not say a word about it. I wish to quote La Presse of April 2, 1960:
First surplus for the old age security fund.
For the first time since its establishment in 1951, the old age security fund will have a surplus in 1960-61, Mr. Fleming announced in his budget speech.
This is due to the tax increases enacted last year and which became effective in April in the case of the sales tax, and in July in the case of personal and corporation income taxes (1 per cent).
Due to this tax increase, the deficit in 1959-60 was only $24 million.
In 1960-61, after a full year of increased taxes, the old age security fund will receive $630 million while its payments will reach $590.
The surplus will therefore be about $40 million and overshadow last year's deficit.
From January 1951 to March 1960, the fund accumulated deficits totalling $630 million.
On that amount, over $500 million were paid out of general revenue and in 1954 a sum of about $100 million was charged against the reserve carried under the productive assets account.
My purpose in quoting from various newspapers, Mr. Speaker, was to present a more representative sample of public opinion. That opinion is favourable everywhere. Members of the opposition form the only dissenting group. They are unhappy in Quebec, and none the happier in Ottawa. The population has long been wise as far as Quebec is concerned, and as for Ottawa it has at last become wise to the one-time-great Liberal party, a great party, Mr. Speaker, which has lived to regret its past glory.
In the speech he made in this house on April 8, 1960, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), said that the unemployment insurance fund, which amounted to $874,574,000 in 1957 was down to $408,145,000 in 1960.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, and I am willing to admit that the number of unemployed has increased these last years, and members of the opposition also are willing to admit it, because they know quite well that in 1956 the recession was starting and promised to be worse.
They still remember quite well that they received a report from the economists and that, in order to win the election, they thought it advisable to hide that report somewhere in an office to prevent the people of Canada from knowing that things were looking bad.
The Budget-Mr. English
But on the other hand, it must not be assumed that that increase in the number of unemployed is the only cause of this difference between 800 million and 400 million. It would be more proper to give the facts as they are, without attempting to mislead the public.
I shall therefore point out other facts that have contributed to this reduction.
The period of benefits has been extended from 36 to 52 weeks. This has tended to decrease the unemployment insurance fund. Unemployment insurance for fishermen, which has been in force since the fall of 1957, has greatly contributed to this decrease.
The increase in benefits provided by the present government has also reduced the fund to a great extent.
Moreover, the maximum salary allowing entitlement to benefits has been raised from $4,800 to $5,460 which had the immediate result of increasing by more than 80,000 the number of persons qualifying for unemployment insurance benefits.
Here again, Mr. Speaker, the increase in the number of those in receipt of unemployment insurance has also materially contributed to a decrease in the unemployment insurance fund.
There are also the married women who, formerly, could not get unemployment insurance benefits on account of certain restrictions. The Conservative government has removed all restrictions, so that today all those women can get unemployment insurance benefits like anyone else. There again, Mr. Speaker, that change brought about by the Conservative party, has helped to deplete substantially the unemployment insurance fund.
Mr. Speaker, we have also heard opposition members state here that several industries had closed down. I should like to say a few words about that matter which is, in my opinion, of a very great importance. I shall refer particularly to the province of Quebec and point out to the house that if some industries have shut down, there are several others which, for several years now, have been well rooted in Quebec.
Let us glance at a report entitled:
Industrial Progress 1958
On page 13, we read the following:
Investments in primary industry and construction rose by 21.1 per cent in 1958 compared to the average for the years 1948 to 1957. In 1958, investments in these two industrial fields are estimated at $241,000,000 and represent 9.4 per cent of total investments for the year.

Concrete evidence of the rapid expansion our manufacturing industry is undergoing can be seen in the fact that, during 1958, more than 328 new manufacturing establishments went into operation in the province and 171 existing plants were enlarged during the same 12 months. Several of these are large undertakings. The few listed below represent a total investment in the neighbourhood of $300,000,000.
In proof of this, and to convince my hon. friends of the opposition, here are the names of some of those industries:
(Text):
Canada Iron Foundries Limited, Canadian Steel Foundries, Gattuso Corp., Canadian Car Co. Limited, Proctor and Gamble Co. of Canada Limited, Continental Paper Products, Avon Products Limited, British Petroleum of Canada Limited, Miron et Freres Limitee, Sogemines Consultants Limited, Montreal Cottons Limited, Steel Co. of Canada Limited, Quebec Iron and Titanium Corp., Lignosol Chemicals Limited, Quebec Cartier Mining Co., Walter M. Lowney Limited, Reynolds Aluminum Co. of Canada Limited.
