Mr. Speaker, I believe the situation is not so bad; and while much is being made of the few industries that have closed down, those are things which happen and which will always happen. It should not be said that it is due to the recession. There is one point, however, that we must take into consideration, and that is management. Some people are more experienced in management than others. And bad management may be a. reason for the shut-down of a plant.
I should like also to say a word, Mr.. Speaker, about mines. Here is what we find-in that same report:
Since the end of the war, the province of Quebec's mining industry has expanded to a remarkable degree; in fact, the total value of mineral production rose from $91.6 million in 1945 to $443,808,980 in 1957, an increase of 384.5 per cent. During: the same period, the value of metals increased from $48.1 million to $238.8 million, while that of industrial minerals rose from $29.0 million to $120.6 million, and building materials from $14.4 million to $85.0 million. Around forty thousand workers are employed in various branches of the mineral industry and their total earnings are in excess of $135 million a year. The same industry's expenditures for fuel and electricity amount to more than $50 million a year.
The total value of mineral production in Quebec during 1958 adds up to around $395.6 million, which represents a large increase over the average for the years from 1950 to 1956, which was $299.8 million. Half of this total value or 50.7 per cent represents: that output of metals which reached about $200.4 million; that of industrial minerals was $107.3 million or 27.1 per cent and building materials accounted for 22.3 per cent $87.8 million.
And, Mr. Speaker, I still quote from the same report, where it says:
The mining of iron ore is by far the most important feature in the development of our mineral resources, and although shipping only began in 1954, iron ore has ranked ahead of all other Quebec mining products, from the point of view of value, since 1957. At present, the greater part of our output of iron ore comes from the huge deposits in the area around Schefferville. The working of these deposits necessitated a capital expenditure in the neighbourhood of $250 million.
A 350-mile long railroad had to be built between Schefferville and the shipping port at Seven Islands on the north shore; the mining town of Schefferville, which now has a population of more than 3,000 was erected; two hydroelectric stations were installed to supply power to work the mines and operate the harbour facilities at Seven Islands, where the ore is loaded on board cargo vessels which carry it to the large consuming centres on the great lakes and the Atlantic coast. Between July 31, 1954, and the end of 1957, the Iron Ore Company of Canada shipped around 34 million tons of ore on some 2,228 cargo ships.
Extensive work is being carried on preparatory to the development of large iron ore deposits in the area of Mount Reed, some 160 air miles north of Shelter Bay. This undertaking calls for large scale

projects, including the building of a railway 312 miles in length to link the mines to the North Shore; a shipping harbour at Port Cartier near Shelter Bay; a central electric station on the Hart-Jaune river, as well as two new town sites. One of the most interesting aspects of this project is the establishment by the Quebec Cartier Mining Company of large mills to refine the ore before shipment. The annual output of the mills will be 8 million tons of concentrates grading more than 60 per cent iron.
And, Mr. Speaker, here is what we also find in the same report:
Asbestos produced in 1957 amounted to $93.6 million, or more than the total value of Quebec's mineral output in 1946. About 65 per cent of the asbestos produced in the free world is mined in the province of Quebec. In 1958, three new concerns went into production. At Black lake, Lake Asbestos of Quebec has almost completed the draining of the lake and begun to work the huge deposits under its bed. At the same time Carey Canadian and National Asbestos began to operate their new mills which can produce 2,000 and 3,000 a day respectively. Lake Asbestos of Quebec alone will produce enough asbestos to increase the volume of Canadian production by 10 per cent.
Well, Mr. Speaker, do the facts I quoted not prove that our country's economy is in good condition? If we leave hovering in this house an impression that our industries in Canada are on the verge of bankruptcy, is it not bad publicity, does it not tend to discourage our friends the Americans from setting up industries in Canada?
That is why I wanted to state the facts today and show the real position of our Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, I have made a summary of the budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance, to which I added a few considerations.
I also wanted to point out the economic development of the province of Quebec, a development which is occurring in the other Canadian provinces as well. We would be remiss if we did not tell the truth and give our whole country the publicity which must be given to it by those who are entrusted with its administration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have waited long and patiently to participate in the budget debate, and I and many other Canadians, I believe, are very curious about what took place in the house yesterday. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) spoke in the budget debate and I can agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that he did not say anything particularly important.

Would you understand it?
The Budget-Mr. Peters

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have to ask myself this question. Why did the Minister of Finance rise in his place and take two and a half hours to tell the Canadian people that the Leader of the Opposition had not said anything of any importance and that his criticism was not valid? This would indicate to me that either the Minister of Finance did give some weight to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition or he became so impressed with his own importance and liked to hear himself speak so much that he spoke for two and a half hours.
Are you looking in a mirror?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It was not necessary for the Minister of Finance to do this on this occasion because he has proved in the past that he can speak at great length and that he has the ability to carry on a discussion of financial matters without saying anything new. He does not have to prove that.
We have had three budget speeches this year, two by the minister and one by his parliamentary secretary. I would have thought that in these three budget speeches we would have been able to find something to justify to some extent a feeling of exhilaration among the Canadian people as to benefits they could hope to receive. This may have been true for a very few people in the civil service but it is not true for many other people.
If we want to solve many of the financial problems facing Canada today I suggest we can do no better than to call on the Minister of Finance to resign and be replaced by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) who in speaking in the budget debate made a number of proposals that certainly were satisfactorily documented. He also did something that the minister has always failed to do. He pointed out that somebody is going to have to pay for increased benefits and that the money is going to have to come from some place. He went on to point out how the money could be raised.
It was interesting to listen to the remarks of the previous speaker. He pointed out that it was wonderful that the minister had been able to bring in a balanced budget and forecast a surplus of $12 million. He said that it was a most wonderful thing that some civil servants were going to get a raise and that the government was still going to be able to hang on to the $12 million. We all know that this is not correct. We all know that you cannot maintain the tax structure and increase benefits to the people.
We listened to the same argument last year with respect to increasing unemployment insurance benefits. Certainly we increased them

The Budget-Mr. Peters but we only increased them for about one-third of the people while at the same time greatly increasing the premiums paid by everybody coming under the scheme. This year we have a balanced budget but how is it being balanced? It is being balanced through the simple expedient of not giving to the common people in Canada the things that they need and deserve. I speak of the veterans who are in need of an increase in their pensions. Increased family allowances are necessary to maintain the standard of living for the children of this country. I speak of the old age pensioners for whom a new form of contribution must be devised so that we can continue to increase old age pensions as needed.
We also balanced this budget at the expense of the farmers and the unemployed of this country. For example, in the matter of family allowances, hon. members will recall that the rates were set in 1945, and they were raised in 1957. We also remember that at the time they were raised in 1957 almost half of the categories were changed so that, in actual fact, only about half of those receiving family allowances received any benefit from the change. It seems to me the time has arrived when we should be again supplying families the amount we originally set in 1945.
I believe that in so far as the veterans are concerned, everybody in the veterans affairs committee agrees that the pension needs to be increased. I do not believe there is anybody in the committee who disagrees with that view. We have been hearing these same people agree with this view for three years now and yet nothing has happened. Elmore Philpott, writing in the Vancouver Sun, had this to say:
When Canada set up the very first war veterans pension scheme back in 1919, the stated fundamental principle was very simple. It was that the basic rate of full pension for a single man was to be equal to the going pay of a day labourer. That is what was then commonly called a "pick-and shovel man". We took over this fair principle from the British.
Then he goes on to show how this has actually worked over the years. In 1919 the civilian wage was $900 and the pension was $900; in 1948 the civilian wage was $2,080 and the pension, $1,128; in 1952 the civilian wage, $2,810 and the pension $1,500; in 1957 the civilian wage was $3,520 and the pension remained at $1,800.
Notwithstanding the three substantial increases which were given from 1948 to 1957, the disabled war veteran is getting less than half of what all parties agreed to in 1919 as the fair and reasonable basis.

I wonder if the hon. member knows that the same Mr. Philpott he is

quoting is the gentleman who voted against an increase in veterans' pensions which I recommended and moved in the committee in 1952?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I did not know that, and I certainly accept the minister's correction. However, this does not in any way change the accuracy of what I am quoting, and I am in complete agreement with these statements.
I can tell the hon. member that what he is quoting is quite incorrect.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to finish this quotation:
Nobody in any government or party planned to make the disabled war veteran the victim of the process of creeping inflation, but that is how it has worked out.
I do not think this is incorrect. The minister may have quarrelled with the amount, but in days gone by I believe we agreed that a pensioner who was getting a 100 per cent pension, whether it was a war pension, old age pension or a pension granted in compensation by the various provinces, should get a pension that bore some relationship to civilian wages of the day. I am not sure whether the minister agrees that is the relationship. The value of these pensions has decreased very rapidly until today pensioners, particularly those from the first war, are not getting enough to enable them to live. I think this is the type of consideration that has been given that has allowed the Minister of Finance to balance the budget.
When the hon. member for Kootenay West was speaking in this budget debate he said it is true that the C.C.F. has always been desirous of a balanced budget. However, we do not believe in balancing the budget at the expense of the Canadian people. There are times, and there will continue to be times, when it is necessary to spend money to create work that is necessary to provide jobs. The full use of the productive assets of our country is the only way to have a balanced budget or to have a satisfactory arrangement so far as the Canadian people themselves are concerned.
I should like to go on to another matter which relates to a letter put out by a club in British Columbia, and I think it should be brought to the minister's attention. I believe conditions might develop that would not be advantageous to the Canadian people, and I do not think they will be advantageous or fair to the particular baseball club that is affected. This letter refers to the Mounties, a well known baseball club in Vancouver, and refers to the fact that you can buy tickets to the various games, the cost of

which will be deductible for income tax purposes. Here is what they say in the letter:
Here are the various 1960 plans under which you can buy tickets for business-getting distribution to:
1.	Your best customers
2.	The people you want as customers
3.	Your pro-company employees
I do not believe we can agree that you should be able to establish non-union employees, company stooges and the like, by allowing the cost of baseball tickets to be deductible for income tax purposes and allowing the tickets to be used to accomplish these purposes. This is something at which the minister must take a look. I am quite sure he would be willing to give consideration to changing this provision.
One of the special budget speeches was the one made by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) this year. He commented on the civil service and made a number of statements as to what he thought would be satisfactory to a large number of these civil servants. I should like now to deal with the salary policy of the government as mentioned by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, and also by his parliamentary secretary. These increases cover only 43,500 out of roughly 170,000 classified civil servants. While these increases are certainly a step in the right direction, when they are looked at in relation to the whole civil service they must be described as a small step indeed.
There is grave doubt among many civil servants as to exactly what their position is regarding salary adjustments. I have carefully followed this issue, and in particular the demands of organized civil servants. I must say that I have been somewhat surprised at the restraint they have shown and also the reasonableness of their requests. As you know, the tendency in private industry is to seek flat, across the board increases. However, I should like to draw your attention to a submission made to the Minister of Finance on February 24 by the joint action committee of the public service organizations. This is the organization described by an hon. member opposite as one led by a group of bludgeoning, bullying leaders. This is a statement that is a little difficult to rationalize with the tempered and reasoning arguments put forward at all times by these people.
In that statement to the Minister of Finance there was no question whatsoever of a flat across the board increase. The committee made certain points which in my opinion are worthy of noting again. They are as follows:
(1)	That the civil service commission recommendations-whatever they may be-in their latest salary report should be implemented.
The Budget-Mr. Peters
(2)	Priority should be given in the budget tc providing the funds necessary to raise the level of civil service salaries to a position of comparability with the salaries of employees in private industry, a position that few classes in the service even begin to approach.
(3)	That the government undertake to maintain civil service salaries at levels comparable to those in private industry by regular adjustments to any classification, or group of classes, shown to be 3 per cent or more behind comparable industrial salary levels.
Where in these statements is there any reference to flat across the board increases? Where is there any attempt to bludgeon the government? It has always been my view as an observer and one who has had experience in industrial negotiations that the civil servants in this country generally have asked for no more than fair and equitable treatment from us their employers. Has the Minister of Finance given them this in his overcautious budgetary announcement? I think not.
Let us look at what has been done to date. I emphasize that promises will not pay the rent, that implied increases for others will not meet doctors' bills, and that many civil servants are frankly concerned as to exactly what is their position regarding adjustments of their salaries. The government in its wisdom has arbitrarily selected April 1, 1960 as the date for adjusting salaries. Yet the present salary anomaly was proved to exist as far back as October 1, 1958.
This is not a matter of my opinion or the opinion of any association, but the result of study by parliament's own agency, the civil service commission through its pay research bureau. This means that even including those who have received increases effective April 1, every civil servant in this country has sustained an average loss in salary of anywhere from $500 to $800 for the period. This, in effect, amounts to additional taxation. I suggest this is another means by which the minister achieved a balanced budget.
The super caution on the part of the Minister of Finance in making piecemeal adjustments has only tended to cause unease, trepidation and wonderment in the minds of many civil servants. There are 45,000 relatively happy civil servants today but there are another 125,000 who do not know exactly what to expect. Great anomalies have been created by this announcement. There are offices today where supervisory employees with heavy responsibilities are being paid

The Budget-Mr. Peters less than those who work under them. Technical, administrative and professional employees have seen traditional relativities destroyed by this piecemeal approach.
Hon. members who have studied the make-up of the civil service will recognize that it is a highly stratified society. Each class is divided into grades, and each grade on the scale is paid a higher salary than the one immediately under it. Such stratification means that there is considerable prestige attached to the position held. This prestige is part of the supervisory system and it is necessary if proper efficiency and discipline is to be maintained. Reduce the dollar spread and the whole structure is out of proportion.
The government must move with haste to restore the proper relationship between the various grades and classes. It is only fair that those civil servants in administrative and technical positions who have not received adjustment now feel that the government is completely unconcerned with maintaining or *restoring the proper salary and supervisory relationships and differential in the various areas of the civil service. However, this particular situation is really not the true illness of government-staff relationships, but rather a symptom of something much deeper.
First of all, I think each and every hon. member of this house must accept some share of responsibility for the situation as it exists. How many of us have taken the time and trouble to truly study the problems of employment in the government service? How many of us have tried with sympathy to [DOT]understand the position of the civil servant .and his associations? How many hon. members actually have underlying feelings of resentment toward the civil servant and his organization for reasons that to me are *vague? How many have truly studied the need for an effective system of collective bargaining within the government service? How many have taken the trouble to listen objectively to the viewpoint of the organizations? If we had, the present unsatisfactory salary situation of the moment would never have occurred. Does the government recognize the legitimate desire of government employees to have a form of negotiation that is honourable and fair to the employee, while at the same time protecting the rights of parliament in money matters.
I have taken the trouble to study the position of the associations on collective bargaining. Nowhere do I see them demanding the right to strike. In fact, none of the major organizations have suggested that the same legislation applying to the industrial situation should also apply to the civil service. With some minor exceptions, civil servants

have no desire to strike or usurp the traditional and legal functions of this parliament to vote money to carry on the country's business. Nor have I seen any desire on the part of civil servants, either individually or through their organizations, to assume cabinet or management functions. To the contrary, they have never asked for anything more than a fair and equitable system that will permit them to sit down with their employer and discuss as equals the terms and conditions of their employment.
In the near future hon. members will be asked to consider a new Civil Service Act. The organized civil servants strongly believe that within the framework of this act there must appear legal provision for collective bargaining. I have not been impressed with the provisions of appendix B of the Heeney report. It is naive in its assumptions and, to my understanding, it completely ignores the legitimate aspirations of the employees. It has all the weaknesses of a unilateral compromise in that it fails completely to appreciate the need for participating in employment matters that now exist. It is too much concerned with maintaining outmoded traditional concepts that are useless in 1960.
There are definite precedents for bargaining for civil servants. The government of Saskatchewan has negotiated with its employees for 15 years. In Great Britain the Whitley system has worked well for many years. In Australia and New Zealand a form of negotiation has been worked out that does not for one moment usurp any of the rights or privileges of the government or parliament, but has provided the employees with a fair and honourable means of collectively solving their problems. In certain so-called backward countries government employees enjoy these rights.
How much longer can we keep our heads in the sand? Collective bargaining is an accepted fact of life today. Even the most reactionary private employers have accepted collective bargaining as being here to stay. This parliament has passed legislation to ensure that citizens at large, excluding our own civil servants, may organize and bargain collectively with their employers. Legislation in practically all provinces provides the same rights. By what logic, by what right, can parliament and the government deny its own employees the proper and accepted means of settling their employment problems in an honourable and dignified way?
Time will not stand still. Collective bargaining for government employees is inevitable. It cannot be achieved by unilateral decision but through a spirit of co-operation

and honesty by the government and civil servants and their organizations. A fair method can and must be worked out. It is time that the government and hon. members recognized that organizations in the civil service are here to stay and that they cannot be treated as evils to be tolerated but not recognized. Common sense dictates such an approach. The civil service is vital to the country's welfare. It must be well paid and provided with proper bargaining procedures if its efficiency and loyalty is to be maintained.
We have been pointing out that there are a number of factors involved in the opportunity the minister took to balance his budget. We believe the budget has been balanced at the sacrifice of the Canadian people and that this type of balanced budget is not necessarily in the interests of the Canadian people. We believe that consideration must be given to all the civil servants. Consideration must be given to retroactivity in our dealings with the civil service if we are going to operate in the manner in which we have operated in the past. We believe that consideration must also be given to the increasing of old age pensions, family allowances and veterans' benefits because these people are the victims in every case, as are all those with fixed incomes, of inflation for which this government is entirely responsible. Mr. Speaker, these are factors which must be taken into consideration in balancing the budget.
In conclusion I want to stress that this budget takes no account of the needs of the recipients of old age pensions, the needs of the civil servants and the needs of others with fixed incomes. It fails to indicate any government plan to deal with the chronic unemployment situation or with our depressed areas such as Elliot Lake, and other places. It fails to offer any plan for dealing with our trade imbalance and with the potentially high, I might say dangerous, influx of foreign equity capital into Canada. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, this group will oppose this budget.

subtopic: FREE PORT PROPOSALS, MORTIER BAY, NFLD.
FREE PORT PROPOSALS, MORTIER BAY, NFLD.
speechtext:
1.	Have any proposals been submitted to the government of Canada for the establishment of (a) a free port and/or (b) a transshipment port at Mortier bay, Newfoundland?
2.	If so, what is the nature of those proposals and from whom were they received?
3.	If not, is the government giving any consideration to the possibility of bringing such a project into being?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister
of Transport):
1.	The government has received a request that it finance an investigation of the engineering, economic, and financial aspects of a project to establish a transshipment port at Mortier bay, Newfoundland.
2.	The request was made by H. D. MacKenzie and C. F. MacLellan of Toronto, on behalf of The Mortier Bay Development Company Limited, a company incorporated under the laws of Newfoundland.
3.	The government having had a careful study made of the proposal decided to take no action.

1.	How many inmates are there in solitary confinement in each of the penitentiaries built by the federal government?
2.	Has any inmate now in solitary confinement been so confined for a period in excess of one year? If so, how many, and for what lengths of time has each of them already spent in solitary confinement?
3.	Does the government enforce the legislation forbidding penitentiary employees from taking additional outside employment?
4.	In how many penitentiaries are members of the medical profession permitted to operate a practice outside of their civil service duties?
5.	In how many penitentiaries is provision made for a separate and distinct office for the work of the employees of the John Howard society?
Answer by: Hon. E. D. Fullon (Minister of
Justice):
1. Penitentiary inmates are not kept in solitary confinement. In each institution there is a block of cells where inmates are dissociated from the rest of the population for disciplinary or administrative reasons. As of December 31, 1959 the number of inmates so dissociated was as follows:
Dorchester penitentiary	 3
St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary .	5
Kingston penitentiary	 8
Manitoba penitentiary	 2
Saskatchewan penitentiary		2
British Columbia penitentiary ...	2
Total	 22
Questions
2.	As of December 31, 1959 three inmates had been so dissociated for more than one year as follows: 1 since June 1954, 1 since August 1956, 1 since April 1958.
3.	In common with other civil servants, penitentiary employees are not precluded from accepting part-time employment in their off-duty hours, so long as such employment does not interfere with their efficiency in the carrying out of the duties of their normal employment.
4.	Penitentiary physicians at Dorchester, federal training centre, Kingston, Collin's Bay, Joyceville, Saskatchewan and British Columbia penitentiaries are permitted to carry on a practice outside their civil service duties under the terms of their employment.
5.	At no penitentiary are separate and exclusive offices provided for the representatives of the John Howard societies. Adequate provision is made at all penitentiaries for the interviewing of inmates by the representatives of the various organizations concerned with the rehabilitation of inmates.
